newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wine industry braces for Nino.
newsitem.headline: Australian wine industry braces for Nino.

text.p: The Australian wine industry is steeling itself for a possible lower grape crop in 1998 due to a developing El Nino weather pattern, historically linked to drought in eastern Australia. (corrects crop year)

But experts said the grape crop was unlikely to be cut as much as in 1994, when El Nino contributed to between a 15 to 20 percent fall in production in vineyards across eastern and southern Australia.
"An El Nino event could certainly have an impact in the order of 10 percent," Glen Cunningham, a spokesman for wine and packaging group Southcorp Ltd told Reuters.
But Cunningham said the chance of grape output falling by more than 10 percent in 1998 was small. (corrects crop year)
"The 1995 vintage (from the 1994 crop) was the worst in 20 years. The severity of it was its widespread impact," he said.
Ray King, chief executive of Fosters Brewing Group Ltd wine unit Mildara Blass Ltd, said El Nino was only one of a number of factors that affected the 1994 grape crop.
"My guess is that the deficit in the 1995 vintage was probably 30 percent due to drought and 70 percent due to other factors," King told Reuters.
King said the other factors were not necessarily related to the drought conditions and included things like frost, wind and the temperature at the time the grape vine buds were formed.

"There would be 30 or 40 reasons why vines don't produce the grapes they should," he said. "Whilst we would prefer not to have drought conditions it is not a serious issue for the Australian wine industry per se," he said.
The Australian Bureau of Meteorology's long range weather forecasting unit, the National Climate Centre, said the El Nino pattern was now confirmed.
"Most of the (weather) models around the world are indicating now that it (El Nino) will continue during the remainder of the year," National Climate Centre spokeswoman Mary Voice said.
Voice said the strength of the effect was proportionate to the amount of heat energy measured in the Pacific Ocean. The last intense El Nino lasted for about 12 months over 1982 and 1983.
Voice said some wine areas that were affected by the 1994 drought, like the Hunter Valley in New South Wales, were marginal in terms of whether they would be affected by El Nino.
"The coastal region of New South Wales and southern Victoria are sometimes affected and sometimes not," she said.
Southcorp's Cunningham said the company's reduced 1995 vintage was in line with the rest of the market in that year.

"Grapes actually eminate from a mediterranean environment. What they are used to is cool wet winters and hot dry summers," he said. "The real issue is if you fail to get winter rain or you don't have sufficient dam capacities at that growth phase."
Cunningham said Southcorp had moved to limit its exposure to volatile rainfall levels by buying vineyards in areas that had more reliable climatic patterns and good water supplies.
"There isn't too much we can do about weather forecasts. What we can do, is manage the key variables," he said.
